sentences.text:
Instant petition under Section 482 Cr.P.C. is filed by the petitioner assailing the impugned order of cognizance dated 30th March, 2021 passed in G.R. Case No.117 of 2021 by the learned S.D.J.M.,
Cuttack corresponding to Cuttack Mahila P.S. Case No. 10 of 2021 on the grounds inter alia that no offence under Section 376 IPC is made out hence the same is liable to be interfered with.
2. The petitioner has been chargesheeted under Sections 376(2)(n) IPC besides other allied offences.
Later to the chargesheet filed against the petitioner, the learned court below took cognizance of the alleged offences vide the impugned order dated 30th March, 2021 (Annexure-3).

According to the petitioner, considering the FIR and other materials submitted along with the chargesheet does not make out a charge of rape, however, the learned court below took cognizance of the said offence which is bad in law.
Rajendra Rayaguru Vrs. State of Odisha and Another 3.

Mr. Rath, learned counsel for the petitioner submits that opposite party No.2 lodged the FIR (Annexure-1) stating therein that she is a married lady and developed relationship with the petitioner.
It is alleged by opposite party No.2 that the petitioner forcibly kept physical relationship and committed other overt acts.
The details of the mischief committed by the petitioner against her have been narrated in Annexure-1 by opposite party No.2.

After investigation was concluded, the petitioner was chargesheeted for the offences alleged including Section 376(2)(n) IPC which is presently under challenge on the ground that no prima facie case for rape is established even by considering Annexure-1 and the chargesheet.

While contending so, Mr. Rath cited the following decisions, such as, Kaini Rajan Vrs. State of Kerala (2013) 9 SCC 113; Vijayan Vrs. State of Kerala (2008) 14 SCC 763; Pramod Suryabhan Pawar Vrs. State of Maharashtra and Another (2019) 9 SCC 608; Dr. Dhruvaram Murlidhar Sonar Vrs. State of Maharashtra and Others (2019) 18 SCC 191;
Maheswar Tigga Vrs. State of Jharkhand (2020) 10 SCC 108; Sonu @ Subhas Kumar Vrs. State of U.P. and Another 2021 SCC OnLine SC 181; and Sambhu Kharwar Vrs. State of U.P. and Another 2022 SCC OnLine SC 1032 and submitted that the allegation of rape is not made out against the petitioner and therefore, the impugned order under Annexure-3 is not sustainable in law to the aforesaid extent.

Mr. Mishra, learned counsel for the State submits that the consent of opposite party No.2 has been obtained under duress and therefore, the case of rape is prima facie established and Rajendra Rayaguru Vrs. State of Odisha and Another hence, the petitioner has been rightly chargesheeted.

entities.text: Rajendra Rayaguru Vrs. State of Odisha and Another
entities.label: PRECEDENT

sentences.text: The petitioner, according to Mr. Mishra, learned ASC, did the mischief and managed to capture intimate moments shared with opposite party No.2 and also threatened her to make it public unless the physical relationship is continued
and therefore, the consent is no consent in the eye of law.

6. Ms. Mishra, learned counsel for opposite party No.2 submitted that the consent of the victim cannot be presumed which has no validation in the eye of law and despite a consensual relationship which is being claimed whether such consent was valid or not can only be examined at the stage of trial and hence, the petitioner shall have to face the charge under Section 376(2)(n) IPC.

It is contended by Ms. Mishra that the petitioner established sexual relationship with opposite party No.2 by administering the fear of harm to her family members which vitiates the passive consent and hence, an offence of rape can be said to have been committed by him.
7.

In Kaini Rajan (supra), the Supreme Court held that the consent given by the prosecutrix believing the promise of marriage is no consent under misconception of fact unless the accused had no intention to marry her from the very beginning and such promise was offered only to obtain consent for the sexual act in which case it would constitute an offence of rape.

Similarly in Vijayan (supra), the Apex Court concluded that in case of promise to marry and thereafter refusal and delay in registering the complaint by the victim concluded that it would be unsafe to convict the accused for an offence under Section 376 IPC unless supported by clinching evidence.

In Dr. Dhruvaram Murlidhar Sonar (supra), it is observed that consensual involvement between the parties without there being any misconception created by the accused Rajendra Rayaguru Vrs. State of Odisha and Another does not constitute rape.

It is further held therein that the victim's conscious decision to be involved in sexual relation with the accused without pressure and misconception and the relationship not involving passive submission of the victim, an offence of rape would not made out Rajendra Rayaguru vs State Of Odisha And Another .... ... on 23 March, 2023 Indian Kanoon - http://indiankanoon.org/doc/34990264/

sentences.text: and discussed the finer distinction between rape and consensual sex.
In the said case, the FIR and chargesheet was quashed in the absence of any material in support of the charge of rape and other offences.

In Maheswar Tigga (supra), it has been held that consent if obtained under a false promise of marriage may be a case of no consent in the eye of law and misconception of fact has to be in proximity of time to the occurrence and cannot be spread over a period of four years as it was in the said case and there was also absence of any false promise of marriage to the victim by the accused.

In Pramod Suryabhan Pawar (supra), the Supreme Court laid bare the subtle difference between false promise and breach of promise and held that a misconception of fact arises out of a false promise and in that case, an offence of rape could be alleged.

However, it has been further held therein that consent with respect to Section 375 IPC involves active understanding of circumstances,
action and consequences of proposed act and individual who makes a reason to choice after assessing the situation and various possible outcome amounts to offering consent.

In the said case also, the victim alleged false promise and came out with an allegation of rape and the Apex Court held that the parties had been in sexual relationship spanning over a period of six years and the allegations in the FIR did not in their case indicate that promise was false or that the victim engaged the sexual relation on the basis of such false promise and finally quashed the FIR, a relief which was denied by the High Court.
Rajendra Rayaguru Vrs. State of Odisha and Another 8.

sentences.text: In the present case, on a reading of the FIR as at Annexure-1, it is made to appear that opposite party No.2 is a married lady and she met the petitioner at her husband's medicine shop and thereafter, their friendship and intimacy between them was developed.
It is also revealed that opposite party No.2 gave birth to a girl child on 14th June, 2020, whereafter, the relationship between the two started to have deteriorated.
The alleged affair between the petitioner and opposite party No.2 was learnt by the latter's husband which led to disturbance in her marital life.
The statement of opposite party No.2 under Section 161 Cr.P.C. narrates in detail the circumstances under which her relationship with the petitioner started.
The petitioner however declined the paternity of the girl child born to opposite party No.2 as made to understand from the record.
When the situation worsened, the petitioner is said to have ill-treated opposite party No.2 which is also described by the latter in her statement under Section 161 Cr.P.C.

On a consideration of the entirety of the material on record, the Court finds that the parties developed relationship over a period of time though it was alleged by opposite party No.2 that she was either reluctant or under compulsion to be sexually engaged with the petitioner.

It is also revealed that the petitioner was not in favour of abortion of opposite party No.2 when she became pregnant though he alleged to have denied the paternity of the child and in order to prove the same, the prosecution has moved the court for collection of his blood sample for DNA analysis.
The opposite party No.2 also admitted that the petitioner agreed to accept her once she obtains divorce from her husband and also borne the expenses at the time of delivery of the girl child.

From the statement of opposite party No.2 under Section 161 Cr.P.C. it is also made to appear that after she gave birth to a girl child, the petitioner disowned the Rajendra Rayaguru Vrs. State of Odisha and Another responsibility and did not assist her financially which led to deterioration of their relationship.

sentences.text: Under the facts and circumstances of the present case, whether a case of rape is prima facie made out or not against the petitioner for which he has been chargesheeted.
There is no doubt that opposite party No.2 was ill-treated by the petitioner towards the end of their relationship.

But,
opposite party No.2 is a married lady and she came in contact with the petitioner and thereafter developed relationship which started sometime in the year 2018 and continued till the end of 2020.

It is no doubt alleged that the petitioner prevailed upon opposite party No.2 and sexually exploited her as revealed from Annexure-1 but despite that their relationship continued for which she became pregnant and also gave birth to a girl child in the month of June, 2020, the abortion of which was opposed by the former.

The understanding between the parties till the very end except the allegation that the sexual intimacy was under compulsion or duress remained unaffected as a result of which opposite party No.2 gave birth to a child for which the expenses at the time of delivery was met by the petitioner
, however, thereafter, under the circumstances narrated in Annexure-1, the relationship was broken.
There has been no promise of marriage by the petitioner from the beginning which is not even claimed by opposite party No.2,
Rather, it is asserted by opposite party No.2 that petitioner was ready to accept her after she gets her divorce.
To say that, there was misconception of fact for any such reason does not arise at all as it was without any such promise of marriage being given from inception.
Rather the relationship as it appears was based on a friendship turned to an intimate relationship between the parties which had a troubled ending.

As earlier mentioned, the Rajendra Rayaguru Vrs. State of Odisha and Another victim opposite party No.2 is a married lady and it can therefore be said that she was not fully conscious of the consequences in the event developed any relationship with the petitioner.

entities.text: Rajendra Rayaguru Vrs. State of Odisha
entities.label: PRECEDENT

sentences.text: It is not that the relationship had any such foundation which began with a promise by the petitioner to marry and accept opposite party No.2.
Though the petitioner denied the paternity but according to opposite party No.2, he was averse to abortion and was not inclined in its favour.
Having discussed all such relevant materials, whether it would still be a case of without consent of opposite party No.2.
Can it be said that opposite party No.2 was a passive consenting party which is being claimed by Ms. Mishra, learned counsel appearing on her behalf.

If someone is under compulsion develops a relationship or out of fear engaged in sexual intimacy or for certain reason extraneous for which the relationship had to be entertained, under such circumstances, it could be said that there may absent of consent or it was passive consent.
The direct or passive consent depends on the conduct of the parties engaged in a relationship to decide and determine whether a case of rape is established.

The Court's reply to the question of consent is that opposite party in the facts and circumstances of the case being conscious of the consequences of an extra-marital affair cannot plead absence of it taking refuge of being under duress or compulsion.

Hence keeping in view the totality of the facts and the legal position,
the conclusion is that the petitioner cannot be charged of rape though he liable to face prosecution for other offences.
10. Hence, it is ordered.
11. In the result, the CRLMC stands partly allowed.

Consequently, the impugned order of cognizance dated 30th March, 2021 passed in G.R. Case No.117 of 2021 by the learned S.D.J.M., Rajendra Rayaguru Vrs. State of Odisha and Another Cuttack is quashed vis--vis the offence under Section 376(2)(n) IPC leaving the petitioner to be tried for the rest offences.
